title: El Niño breaks warming records in the Pacific Ocean, foreshadowing more extreme weather to come, UN says
summary: The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels ‌around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on…

image.caption: Wildfires burn through peatland forest in Indonesia in September. El Niño is set to cause more weather havoc like this throughout the planet. (Tatan Syuflana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels ‌around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Wednesday.
Floods in some regions, droughts in others as El Niño continues to gather strength
· Posted: Oct 21, 2026 4:24 PM EDT | Last Updated: 5 minutes ago

The new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong, ​with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about ​3.8 C above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

items: Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

blocks.text: "We have not seen in our records 3.8. We ​have seen around [3 C] in some record El Niños before, ⁠with very substantive ⁠impacts across the world. So we ‌are beyond that limit," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.
Celeste Saulo, World Meteorological Organization secretary-general, is warning of record temperatures during this El Niño. (Sergei Grits/The Associated Press)

El Niño is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle — a climate pattern that influences weather around the world. It tends to ⁠cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.
It is a natural climate ‌pattern and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Niños more intense because the baseline temperature is already higher.
El Niño-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising ​in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.
In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a ⁠lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could ⁠see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.

blocks.text: The WMO and the UN ⁠under-secretary-general ⁠for humanitarian affairs and emergency ​relief coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.

"This El Niño ​is the behemoth, it ⁠is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood," Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.
Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he ⁠said.
